Singular

Plural

Definition

Example in a sentence (sing.)

1

Nominative

buddho

buddhā

The subject of the sentence;
the person or thing doing the action.

buddho teaches the Dhamma.

2

Accusative

The direct object of the action.

He sees buddhaṃ. She asks buddhaṃ.

3

Instrumental

buddhena

buddhehi

The instrument by which an action is done. (Prepositions: by, with, through)

The Dhamma is taught buddhena.

The monk converses buddhena.

4

Dative

buddhāya / buddhassa

buddhānaṃ

The indirect object, the person to whom an action is done; “the recipient”; indicates the purpose and benefit. (Prep.: to, for)

He gave alms-food buddhāya.

They presented a question buddhassa.

5

Ablative

buddhā / smā / mhā / to

buddhehi

Indicates separation, movement, origination, and comparison. (Prep.: from, because, than)

He heard the Dhamma buddhā.

We received the Dhamma buddhasmā.

6

Genitive

buddhassa

buddhānaṃ

Expresses possession and ownership (of)

These are the teachings buddhassa.

7

Locative

buddhe / smiṃ / mhi

buddhesu

The place or time of action; “reference”
(in, on, above, etc., regarding, about, etc.)

We have confidence buddhe.

There are wonderful qualities buddhasmiṃ.

Vocative

buddha

buddhā

Used when addressing someone.

Venerable Buddha, please teach us.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.html:
About this Grammar Guide

This is a simplified grammar guide designed to accompany the Pāḷi texts used in this workshop.
It aims to be clear, accessible, and beginner-friendly, without assuming any prior knowledge of grammar.

The explanations are intentionally brief, and therefore not complete or comprehensive.

Hopefully, the explanations are still accurate and helpful, despite being short and incomplete.

Students are encouraged to consult more detailed grammar references for a full and precise explanation of specific topics.

In this guide, only the most common grammatical forms will be presented, along with their most frequent endings, especially those relevant to the texts selected for this workshop.

For a more comprehensive overview, please refer to the detailed grammar summary handout.

Mor Ifrah

Stress Accent:

  • The default position for the stress accent is the third to last syllable:

exx. sa-ra-ṇa ti-ra-ta-na

vi-na-ya ca-ra-ti

pu-ri-sa ga-ma-na

vi-ca-ra-ṇa su-ga-ta

However, if the second to last syllable is “heavy” (by having a long vowel or being followed by two consonants), the stress accent shifts to it:

Exx. sa-ra-ṇe-su

sam-bud-dho

sections.title: Sandhi
sections.html:
• Sandhi (literally “joining” or “combination”) refers to the phonetic changes that occur at the junction of words or syllables, typically when one word ends and the next begins. These adjustments make speech smoother and are very common.
  • Sandhi also exists in English:
    he will → he’ll; I am → I’m; do not → don’t; is not → isn’t; will not → won’t

Some common sandhi sound changes include:

  • Final short vowel drops before a following vowel
    tena + upasaṅkami (there + approached) → ten’upasaṅkami
    pañca + imāni (five + these) → pañc’imāni
  • Two short vowels merging into a long vowel (a + a → ā, a + u → ū)
    pāṇa + atipāta (life + destruction) → pāṇ’ātipāta
    dhamma + upasaṃhita (connected) → dhamm’ūpasaṃhita
  • The niggahīta (ṃ) changes to match the following consonant
    (ṃ becomes ṅ before k & g; ñ before c & j; n before t & d; m before p & b)
    katamaṃ + ca (what + and) → katamañca
    saṃ + bodhi (complete + awakening) → sambodhi
  • ṃ becomes m before a vowel
    taṃ + api (that + too/also) → tam’pi
  • Doubling of consonants
    an aspirated consonant is doubled with its unaspirated partner: kh → kkh, ph → pph
    pañca + khandhā (five + aggregates) → pañcakkhandhā
  • Insertion of letters between vowels
    na + idaṃ (not + this) → nayidaṃ
    adukkha + asukha (not painful + not pleasant) → adukkhamasukha
  • Change of letters
    su + akkhāto (well + explained) → svākkhāto
    bodhi + aṅga (enlightenment + factor) → bojjhaṅga (i → y before a vowel: bodhy-aṅga; then dhy → jjh)

sections.title: Nouns
sections.html:
• A noun is a word that names a person, place, thing, or idea.
    In Pāḷi, as in English, nouns can refer to concrete objects (kāya – body),
    abstract concepts (pāmojja – joy), places (ārāma – park),
    or living beings (purisa – person).

Nouns in Pāḷi are classified according to:

• Gender: masculine, feminine, and neuter

• Number: singular and plural

• Case: eight grammatical cases – nominative, accusative, instrumental, dative,

ablative, genitive, locative, and vocative

sections.title: Pronouns
sections.html:
• A pronoun is a word that stands in place of a noun.
  • Pronouns are also classified according to gender, number, and case.
  • These are the main types of pronouns:
  • Personal pronouns refer to the speaker or others – ahaṃ (I ), tvaṃ (you).
  • Demonstrative pronouns point to specific things – ayaṃ (this), taṃ (that).
  • Relative pronouns introduce relative clauses – yo (which/who, etc.).
  • Interrogative pronouns are used to ask questions – ko/kiṃ (who? what? which?).

sections.title: Relative Pronouns: ya (which / that [which] / [one] who)
sections.html:
• A relative pronoun is a word that introduces a relative clause — a part of the sentence that gives more information about a noun or pronoun.
    In English, relative pronouns include: who, whom, which, that [which], whose
  • Pāḷi often pairs the relative pronoun ya with a demonstrative pronoun ta to link the two parts of the sentence. Where in English we might say:
    “The book that I read is good.” A corresponding construction in Pāḷi would be something like: “Which book I read — that book is good.” (ya book I read — ta book is good).
    For example:
  • yaṃ aniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ [hoti].
    whatever is anicca, that is dukkha.
  • yo paṭicca-samuppādaṃ passati, so dhammaṃ passati.
    one who sees dependent origination, he sees the Dhamma.

sections.title: Adjectives (vant / ī / (i)ka)
sections.html:
An adjective is a word that describes a noun. It gives more information about the noun, such as its quality, quantity, or state (e.g., big, short, kind).

Besides straightforward adjectives like anicca (below), there are a few other common ways to form adjectives in Pāḷi. Very common are the vant/mant and ī types,
shown below in their declension patterns.

Another common way to form adjectives from nouns is by adding the suffix (i)ka,
for example:

  • kāya (body) → kāyika (bodily)
  • cetas (mind) → cetasika (mental)
  • dhamma → dhammika (righteous; in accordance with the Dhamma)

Unlike nouns, adjectives can take all three genders, and must agree (match) with the noun they describe in gender, number, and case. For example:

  • anicco saṅkhāro – masculine, singular, nominative
  • aniccaṃ rūpaṃ – neuter, singular, nominative/accusative
  • aniccā vedanā – feminine, singular/plural, nominative

sections.html:
A compound is a combination of two or more words that are joined together to create a specific meaning.

In a compound, usually only the final word takes a case ending, while the other words remain in their stem form.

There are 6 types of compounds in Pāḷi:

tappurisa – Case Compound

  • A compound in which the first word is related to the second by a case relationship,
    such as genitive (of), instrumental (by/with), dative (to/for), etc.

English Examples

Pāḷi Examples

tabletop → top of a table

buddha-dhamma → the teaching of the Buddha (genitive)

sunlight → light of the sun

mettā-bhāvanā → the cultivation of mettā (genitive)

toothbrush → brush for teeth

anicca-saññā → the perception of anicca (genitive)

book-learning → learning from books

buddha-bhāsita → spoken by the Buddha (instrumental)

bookcase → case for books

attha-saṃhita → connected with benefit (instrumental)

handwriting → writing with the hand

arañña-gata → gone to the forest (accusative)

arañña-vāsa → living in the forest (locative)

dvanda – Copulative Compound

  • A compound that joins two or more items in a list and is usually translated with “and.”

English Examples

Pāḷi Examples

bitter-sweet → bitter and sweet

dhamma-vinaya → teaching and discipline

push-pull → push and pull

nāma-rūpa → mind and matter

on-off → on and off

ñāṇa-dassana → knowledge and vision

samudaya-vaya → arising and passing away

kammadhāraya – Adjectival Compound

  • A compound in which both parts refer to the same thing;
    the second word is usually a noun, and the first qualifies it, like an adjective.

English Examples

Pāḷi Examples

blackbird

dukkha-vedanā → painful feeling

smartphone

kusala-dhamma → wholesome quality

loudspeaker

mahā-purisa → great man

blueberry

piya-vācā → kind words

small-talk

brahma-cariya → spiritual life

hardcopy

sammā-diṭṭhi → right view

bahubbīhi – Possessive Compound

  • A compound that describes something external to itself and is often used adjectivally.

English Examples

Pāḷi Examples

sweetheart [person]

maraṇa-dhammo [satto] → [a being] who is subject to death

redhead [girl]

passaddha-kāyo [bhikkhu] → [a bhikkhu] whose body is tranquil

bare-foot [man]

mahā-pañño [buddho] → [the Buddha] who has great wisdom

big-mouth [person]

vipariṇāma-dhammā [vedanā] → [a sensation] having the nature of change

five-star [hotel]

kamma-dāyādo [amhi] → [I am] one who has kamma as my inheritance

two-car [garage]

gutta-dvāro [bhikkhu] → [a bhikkhu] whose sense doors are guarded

abyayībhāva – Adverbial Compound

  • An indeclinable compound whose first member is typically an adverb or prefix,
    and which functions as an adverb.

English Examples

Pāḷi Examples

(lives) uptown

yathā-bhūtaṃ → in accordance with reality; as it is

(sits) outside

anu-pubbaṃ → gradually

(goes) underground

paccattaṃ (paṭi + atta) → personally

(runs) superfast

ajjhattaṃ (adhi + atta) → internally

digu – Numerical Compound

  • A compound that begins with a number and is followed by a noun.

English Examples

Pāḷi Examples

bicycle

ti-ratana → the three jewels

tripod

catu-sacca → four truths

pañca-kkhandha → five aggregates

pañca-sīla → five precepts

sections.title: Verbs
sections.html:
A verb is a word that expresses an action, occurrence, or state of being.
Verbs in Pāḷi are conjugated primarily to show:

  • Tense (present, past, future)
  • Person (first, second, or third)
  • Number (singular or plural)
  • Mood (indicative, optative, imperative, etc.)
  • Voice (active or passive)

Each verb has a root, which is modified with various endings and sometimes prefixes to create different forms.

sections.title: The Optative (eyya / e)
sections.html:
Use:

The Optative generally expresses:

• Hypothetical or conditional situations

• Polite requests, suggestions, or instructions

• Wishes or hopes

To translate it, we usually use auxiliary verbs such as would, could, might, may, and should.
For example: so/sā gaccheyya – he/she could go / should go, etc.

Formation:

The Optative is formed by adding the following endings to the stem (base) of the verb
(gacchati → gaccha).

Singular

Plural

3rd person (he / they)

gaccheyya / gacche
/ gacchetha

gaccheyyuṃ

2nd person (you)

gaccheyyāsi / gacche

gacchetha / gaccheyyātha

1st person (I / we)

gaccheyyāmi / gaccheyyaṃ
/ gacche

gaccheyyāma

Examples:

  1. yo ca vassa-sataṃ jīve...
    One may live a hundred years... (jīvati), (p. 7)
  2. na haneyya...
    One should not kill... (hanati), (p. 7)
  3. mā ’vamaññetha puññassa...
    One should not underestimate the good... (avamaññati), (p. 8)
  4. anussaretha sambuddhaṃ...
    You should recollect the Buddha... (anussarati), (p. 12)
  5. atha dhammaṃ sareyyātha.
    Then you should recall the Dhamma... (sarati), (p. 12)
  6. n’āhaṃ evaṃ vadeyyaṃ...
    I would not say... (vadati), (p.16)
  7. ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvatteyya...
    Would lead to harm and suffering... (saṃvattati), (p.16)
  8. vacī-pakopaṃ rakkheyya.
    One should guard against angry speech... (rakkhati), (p. 21)
  9. vācāya sucaritaṃ care.
    One should practice good conduct in speech... (carati), (p. 21)
  10. yaṃ tumhe ... vihareyyātha...
    That you ... would dwell... (viharati), (p. 24)
  11. vo pare ... vadeyyuṃ...
    Others may say to you... (vadati), (p. 25)
  12. yaṃ passe vajja-dassinaṃ...
    One should regard the one who sees your faults... (passati), (p. 27)
  13. niggayha-vādiṃ medhāviṃ, tādisaṃ paṇḍitaṃ bhaje.
    One should associate with such a wise one... (bhajati), (p. 27)
  14. cittaṃ rakkhetha medhāvī...
    Let the wise one guard the mind... (rakkhati), (p. 32)
  15. sammā-paṇihitaṃ cittaṃ, seyyaso naṃ tato kare.
    A mind directed rightly could do more good for oneself than that... (karoti), (p. 33)
  16. yaṃ nūn’āhaṃ ... vihareyyaṃ...
    What if I were to dwell... (viharati), (p. 38)
  17. nayidaṃ rūpaṃ ābādhāya saṃvatteyya...
    This material form would not lead to affliction... (saṃvattati), (p. 46)
  18. jano hareyya vā, ḍaheyya vā...
    [If] people were to carry off ... or burn... (harati, ḍahati), (p. 52)
  19. pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ.
    Bad unwholesome states might invade [him]... (anvāssavati), (p. 55)
  20. puṭṭho ca, na sampāyeyya.
    And if questioned, he could not reply... (sampāyati), (p. 56)
  21. attānaṃ niveseyya yathā bhūri pavaḍḍhati...
    One should conduct oneself so that wisdom increases... (niveseti), (p. 60)
  22. tam enaṃ cakkhumā puriso passeyya...
    A man with good sight would observe it... (passati), (p. 71)
  23. sakkāraṃ n’ābhinandeyya...
    Should not seek delight in honors... (abhinandati), (p. 88)
  24. sato, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vihareyya sampajāno.
    A bhikkhu should dwell aware and clearly comprehending... (viharati), (p. 93)
  25. ātāpinī, pahitattā vihareyyaṃ.
    I might dwell ... ardent, and resolute... (viharati), (p. 108)
  26. ye kho tvaṃ, gotami, dhamme jāneyyāsi...
    Gotamī, those things of which you might know... (jānāti), (p. 108)
  27. gotami, dhāreyyāsi...
    You should bear in mind, Gotamī... (dhāreti), (p. 108)
  28. adhigacche padaṃ santaṃ...
    [The bhikkhu ...] would attain the peaceful state... (adhigacchati), (p. 110)
  29. sace hi so ... mettena cittena phareyya...
    If he were to pervade ... with a mind of mettā... (pharati), (p. 113)

sections.title: The Absolutive (tvā / ya)
sections.html:
Use:

The Absolutive (also known as the Gerund) mainly expresses an action that has been completed prior to the action of the main verb in the sentence.

To translate it literally, we usually use "having" + a past participle.

For example: gantvā – having gone.

Formation:

The absolutive is not conjugated. It is formed by adding the endings (i)tvā / (i)tvāna / ya to the root (gacchati → √gam) or stem (base) of the verb, often with some changes to the root
(√gam → gantvā).

Examples:

  1. attānaṃ upamaṃ katvā... 
    (literally) Having made a comparison to oneself... (karoti), (p. 7)
  2. upasaṅkamitvā, bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā...
    Having approached, having paid homage to the Blessed One... (upasaṅkamati, abhivādeti), (p. 13)
  3. ariya-sāvako adinn’ādānaṃ pahāya...
    The noble disciple, having abandoned the taking of what is not given... (pajahati), (p. 15)
  4. musā-vādaṃ pahāya... 
    Having abandoned false speech... (pajahati), (p. 15)
  5. aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ abhayaṃ datvā...
    Having given to an immeasurable number of beings freedom from fear... (dadāti), (p. 20)
  6. vacī-duccaritaṃ hitvā...
    Having abandoned verbal misconduct... (jahati), (p. 21)
  7. tañ ca puggalaṃ mettā-sahagatena cetasā pharitvā viharissāma...
    We shall dwell having pervaded that person with a mind suffused with mettā... (pharati), (p. 25)
  8. etaṃ puggalaṃ akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā...
    Having made this person emerge from the unwholesome... (vuṭṭhāpeti, causative), (p. 27)
  9. bhagavato sutvā, bhikkhū dhāressanti.
    Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it... (suṇāti), (p. 35)
  10. bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā...
    A bhikkhu, having seen a material form with the eye... (passati), (p. 55)
  11. sotena saddaṃ sutvā...
    Having heard a sound with the ear... (suṇāti), (p. 55)
  12. etaṃ dvedhā-pathaṃ ñatvā...
    Having known this two-way path... (jānāti), (p. 60)
  13. so vedanā pariññāya...
    Having fully understood vedanā... (parijānāti), (p. 64)
  14. evam etaṃ abhiññāya...
    Having known it thus... (abhijānāti), (p. 88)
  15. sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā...
    Having concluded their greetings and cordial talk... (vītisāreti), (p. 90)
  16. ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya...
    Having set (their) body erect... (paṇidahati), (p. 95)
  17. satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā...
    Having established awareness... (upaṭṭhāpeti), (p. 95)

sections.title: The Imperative (tu)
sections.html:
Use:
The Imperative is mainly used to express:

With the 2nd person:

• Requests, commands, or instructions: gacchāhi – go!

With the 1st and 3rd person:
• Wishes and hopes (somewhat similar in meaning to the optative):

gacchantu – may they go.

Formation:

The Imperative is formed by adding the following endings to the stem of the verb.

Singular

Plural

3rd person (he / they)

gacchatu

gacchantu

2nd person (you)

gaccha / gacchāhi

gacchatha

1st person (I / we)

gacchāmi

gacchāma

Examples With the Second Person:

  1. akusalaṃ, bhikkhave, pajahatha.
    Bhikkhus, abandon the unwholesome!... (pajahati), (p. 16)
  2. kusalaṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvetha.
    Bhikkhus, develop the wholesome!... (bhāveti), (p. 16)
  3. tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha...
    Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely... (suṇāti, karoti), (p. 35)
  4. yaṃ, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ, taṃ pajahatha.
    Bhikkhus, that which is not yours, let go of it... (pajahati), (p. 52)
  5. jhāyatha, bhikkhave, mā pamād’attha.
    Meditate, bhikkhus, do not be negligent... (jhāyati, atthi), (p. 92)
  6. tasmātih’ānanda, atta-dīpā viharatha...
    Therefore, Ānanda, dwell with yourselves as your own island... (viharati), (p. 100)
  7. tattha ca nimittaṃ gaṇhāhi.
    And take up the object there... (gaṇhati), (p. 107)
  8. appamādena sampādetha...
    Strive without heedlessness to attain [the goal]... (sampādeti), (p. 109)

Examples With the First and Third Person:

  1. upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu.
    Let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower... (dhāreti), (p. 24)
  2. evaṃ me rūpaṃ hotu...
    Let my material form be thus... (hoti), (p. 46)
  3. bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetu.
    Let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief... (deseti), (p. 108)
  4. sabbe bhadrāni passantu.
    May all beings meet (see) with good fortune... (passati), (p. 114)
  5. ahaṃ avero homi.
    May I be free of hatred... (hoti), (p. 116)
  6. ... averā hontu.
    May [my mother ... and everyone] be free of hatred... (hoti), (p. 116)
  7. sukhī attānaṃ pariharantu.
    May they keep themselves happy... (pariharati), (p. 116)
  8. sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhit’attā.
    May they be inwardly happy!... (bhavati), (p. 117)
  9. bhavatu sabba-maṅgalaṃ.
    May there be a true blessing for all beings... (bhavati), (p. 117)

sections.title: The Infinitive (tuṃ)
sections.html:
Use:

The Infinitive mainly expresses the purpose, ability, or suitability of an action and depends on the main verb of the sentence.
It does not indicate time, and is usually translated as “to [verb]” in English.
For example: gantuṃ – to go, passituṃ – to see.

Formation:

The Infinitive is not conjugated. It is formed by adding the ending (i)tuṃ to the root
(gacchati → √gam) or to the stem of the verb (gacchati → gaccha), often with some changes to the root.

Examples:

  1. sakkā, bhikkhave, akusalaṃ pajahituṃ.
    It is possible to abandon the unwholesome... (pajahati), (p. 16)
  2. sakkā, bhikkhave, kusalaṃ bhāvetuṃ.
    It is possible to develop the wholesome... (bhāveti), (p. 16)
  3. sakkomi c’āhaṃ etaṃ puggalaṃ ... kusale patiṭṭhāpetuṃ.
    I am able to establish this person in the wholesome... (patiṭṭhāpeti), (p. 27)
  4. atha kho māro ... bhayaṃ ... uppādetu’kāmo, samādhimhā cāvetu’kāmo...
    Then Māra desiring to arouse fear ... desiring to make her fall away from concentration... (uppādeti, cāveti), (p. 50)
  5. anujānāmi, bhikkhave, imāni ... mettena cittena pharituṃ.
    I enjoin you, bhikkhus, to pervade these ... with a mind of mettā... (pharati), (p. 113)

sections.title: The Past Tense (Aorist)
sections.html:
Use:

The Aorist is mainly used as a past tense in Pāḷi, similar to how the past tense is used in English.

For example: so/sā agacchi – he/she went.

There are several sets of endings for the Aorist, but here they are grouped together selectively to show the most common forms, especially those found in the texts selected for this workshop.

Formation:

The Aorist is formed by adding the following endings to the root (gacchati → √gam),
or stem of the verb (gaccha). In some cases, a short a is added at the beginning.

Singular

Plural

3rd person (he / they)

(a)gacchi / (a)gami / agamāsi

gacchiṃsu / gacchuṃ /
(a)gamaṃsu / gamiṃsu / gamuṃ

2nd person (you)

(a)gacchi / (a)gami / agamāsi

gacchittha / gamittha / agamattha

1st person (I / we)

(a)gacchiṃ / gamiṃ / agamāsiṃ

gacchimha / gamimha

Examples:

  1. mahānāmo sakko yena bhagavā ten’upasaṅkami...
    Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One... (upasaṅkamati), (p. 13)
  2. mahānāmo sakko bhagavantaṃ etad avoca...
    Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One... (vadati / √vac, irregular), (p. 13)
  3. ekam antaṃ nisīdi...
    He sat down to one side... (nisīdati), (p. 17)
  4. byantam eva naṃ akāsiṃ...
    I put (made) an end to it... (karoti), (p. 39)
  5. bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanduṃ...
    The bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s statement... (abhinandati), (p. 49)
  6. gāthāya ajjhabhāsi...
    He addressed her in verse... (ajjhabhāsati), (p. 50)
  7. māro pāpimā ... dukkhī dummano tatthev’ antaradhāyi...
    Then Māra the Evil One ... sad and disappointed, disappeared right there... (antaradhāyati), (p. 50)
  8. tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi...
    There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus... (āmanteti), (p. 57)
  9. bhikkhūnaṃ anupādāya āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsu...
    The minds of the bhikkhus were liberated from the āsavas by non-clinging... (vimuccati), (p. 58)
  10. anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimucci...
    [Bāhiya’s] mind was liberated from the āsavas by non-clinging.... (vimuccati), (p. 59)
  11. antam akāsi dukkhassa...
    He put (made) an end to dukkha... (karoti), (p. 64)
  12. te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ...
    Those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One... (paṭissuṇāti), (p. 66)
  13. sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā ten’upasaṅkamiṃsu...
    A number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One... (upasaṅkamati), (p. 113)
  14. te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etad avocuṃ...
    Those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One... (vadati / √vac, irregular), (p. 113)
  15. anuttaro dhamma-varaṃ adesayi...
    The unsurpassed one taught the excellent Dhamma... (deseti), (p. 115)

sections.title: The Future Tense (issa)
sections.html:
Use:

The Future Tense in Pāḷi expresses the simple future, similar to how it’s used and understood in English. For example: so/sā gacchissati – he/she will go.

Formation:

The future is formed by adding the affix (i)ssa to the stem of the verb (gacchati → gaccha),
or its root (gacchati → √gam), followed by the present indicative endings.

Singular

Plural

3rd person (he / they)

gacchissati

gacchissanti

2nd person (you)

gacchissasi

gacchissatha

1st person (I / we)

gacchissāmi

gacchissāma

Examples:

  1. na maṃ taṃ āgamissati.
    That will not come to me... (āgacchati), (p. 8)
  2. hit’ānukampī ca viharissāma metta-cittā...
    Compassionate for their welfare, we shall dwell with a mind of mettā... (viharati), (p. 25)
  3. iti mayhañ ca avihesā bhavissati...
    For me there will be no trouble... (bhavati), (p. 27)
  4. ariyaṃ aṭṭh’aṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvessati...
    He will develop the Noble Eightfold Path... (bhāveti), (p. 34)
  5. bhagavato sutvā, bhikkhū dhāressanti...
    Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it... (dhāreti), (p. 35)
  6. tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmi...
    Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely, I will speak... (bhāsati), (p. 35)
  7. yaṃ kammaṃ karissāmi — kalyāṇaṃ vā pāpakaṃ vā — tassa dāyādo bhavissāmi.
    Whatever kamma I will do, good or bad, of that I will be the heir... (karoti, bhavati), (p. 40)
  8. taṃ vo pahīnaṃ, hitāya sukhāya bhavissati.
    When it has been let go of by you, [it] will be for your welfare and happiness... (bhavati), (p. 52)
  9. sabbaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi.
    Bhikkhus, I will teach you the all... (deseti), (p. 56)
  10. aññaṃ sabbaṃ paññāpessāmi...
    I shall make known another all... (paññāpeti), (p. 56)
  11. diṭṭhe diṭṭha-mattaṃ bhavissati...
    In the seen there will be merely the seen... (bhavati), (p. 59)
  12. paṭicca-samuppādaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi...
    Bhikkhus, I will teach you dependent origination... (deseti), (p. 74)
  13. satipaṭṭhānañ ca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi...
    Bhikkhus, I will teach you the establishment of awareness... (deseti), (p. 99)
  14. asaṅkhatañ ca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi...
    Bhikkhus, I will teach you the unconditioned... (deseti), (p. 105)

sections.title: Participles
sections.html:
• A participle is a word derived from a verb that retains some verbal qualities but can function in various ways, often as an adjective.

As such, it is declined in all three genders and must agree with the noun it describes in gender, number, and case.

sections.title: The Past Participle (ta / na)
sections.html:
Use:

The Past Participle (pp) is a verbal form that expresses a completed action.
It often describes a noun that has undergone the action, and is typically passive in meaning.

Past Participles in English often end in -ed:

closed, cleaned, relaxed, cooked, washed, printed

Or -en:

eaten, frozen, forgotten, written, broken, spoken, chosen

Formation:

The Past Participle is usually formed by adding the endings (i)ta/na to the root of the verb (gacchati → √gam), often with some changes to the root (√gam → gata).

sections.title: The Present Participle (anta / māna)
sections.html:
Use:

The Present Participle (prp) is a verbal form that expresses an action that is currently happening or ongoing. It often describes a noun that is performing the action, and is typically active in meaning.

Present Participles in English end in -ing :

going, seeing, doing, speaking, eating, walking, sitting

Formation:

The Present Participle is usually formed by adding the ending anta /māna to the stem of the verb (gacchati → gaccha).

The following paradigm shows only the anta endings.
The māna forms follow a very similar declension pattern (gacchamāno, gacchamānaṃ, etc.). The ending māna is also used for passive present participles (e.g. vuccamāna, ‘being called’).

sections.title: The Future Passive Participle (or ptp) (tabba / anīya / eyya)
sections.html:
Use:

The Future Passive Participle (also known as the Potential Participle, ptp)
is a verbal form that expresses something that should or is to be done in the future
(somewhat similar in meaning to the Optative).

It generally indicates that an action is recommended or required, and has a passive meaning.

It is often translated with "to be" + a past participle:

to be done, to be said, to be known, etc.

Formation:

The Future Passive Participle is most often formed by adding the affixes tabba /anīya / eyya
to the stem of the verb (gacchati → gaccha), or its root (gacchati → √gam).

sections.title: Adverbs (aṃ / ena)
sections.html:
• An adverb describes how, when, where, or to what extent something happens.
    It most often modifies a verb, but can also describe adjectives or other adverbs.
    Examples: speaks kindly, waits patiently, comes often.
  • Adverbs are indeclinable, meaning they do not change according to case,
    gender, or number, but remain in the same form.
  • Adverbs in Pāḷi often end in -aṃ /-ena :
    evaṃ (thus), sukhaṃ (happily), sādhukaṃ (well; carefully), bahulaṃ (often),
    khemaṃ (safely), abhiṇhaṃ (frequently), saṅkhittena (briefly),
    kālena (at the proper time)

    But also:
    sammā (fully; rightly), idha (here), yattha (where), tattha (there), yadā (when),
    tadā (then)
